rationale: B wins because it protects the founder from the expensive lie hiding in the shiny number: "whether the 10% applies to subscriptions bought inside the iOS and Android apps." A has good instincts, but it gets loose with "in range with Patreon and Twitch" and "Millions of Unpaid Gaming Community Managers," which are exactly the unsupported shortcuts a reporter will gut first. Both sets find the right broad shapes; B asks the question that decides whether the lead angle survives.
gaps_in_A: "in range with Patreon and Twitch" invents a competitor comparison the update did not supply. You can ask for that data, but you cannot treat it as already true.
"ongoing regulatory scrutiny of app store fees globally keeps this topic warm" is a fake news peg in this record. The update gave a launch, not a live regulatory hook.
"Millions of Unpaid Gaming Community Managers Just Got a Business Model" overclaims twice: "millions" and "unpaid" are not in the facts.
"first real monetization product" is sloppy against Discord's broader business. The update supports a new creator-subscription product, not Discord discovering revenue for the first time.
gaps_in_B: "What a gaming-community server can now charge for, and what stays free" assumes a free-tier framing the update does not actually give. It is a good reporting question, not a settled headline yet.

"The community server becomes the creator's paywall" is the weakest kept angle because it tries to turn one launch into a trend. B knows this and asks for comparable data, but the angle still needs that data before anyone should lead with it.
"whether Discord is in a quiet period" is a useful caution, but it may be legally premature if the IPO prep is only reported and no filing exists. Keep it as a question, not implied fact.
